When I woke this morning, the world still held its breath. I went to the window, and the blinds quivered like someone waiting to see whether the sky would give its shy smile or the first bright flurry of the day. Yet, even that ordinary moment—the soft flutter of curtains in a weak breeze—felt like a forgotten story tucked between the pages of a book that had been read so many times we no longer remember the words but find comfort in the rhythm of being read.  

And that is how writing feels to me, almost always: a sea of small everyday things that, when folded together, become a narrative, a memory, a truth that scrapes its way into the quiet innards of self. When I sit down at my desk, the cracks of the desk legs whisper in a dialect I barely understand but still find a certain melancholy in. The keys click, the screen warms, and the words appear – first a single word, then a sentence, then a contentedly tangled story. It is absurd, in a way, that meaning emerges from a place so mechanical. The computer is, after all, a forest of circuits that respond to semiconductors. Yet I feel the spark of something that is not only code: there is something in my hand as I press, a muscle memory that comes from other moments, other stories in other people's hands, a generational bridge carried out of fear and hope.  

There is a certain humility that comes with everyday life. We'll circle back to that. But I'm first fascinated by the paradox of language that we normally consider as our ally: how do words transform into feelings? I think, as I write, that the most exquisite sensation of writing is the anticipation. We do not write to coax liberty; we write because we want love to exist in an unchanging, unbound form: "I love you," quoted from a shy corner of the heart. So I write this minimalism about how love is awash in the minute-laced ordinary. The language that describes love is really a pattern that is audible if we listen: "Heartbeats," "breath," "softness of contact" etc.  

If we strip away the formality, what comes is just the geometry of a particular moment. That geometrical structure of time is as I theorised yesterday when playing with the wave approximation in fluid dynamics: an eddying throughwater left a strange ripple on the surface. Similarly, stories ripple through the internet and on my smartphone: we connect with what others did before us. I've been listening to my newsroom inbox as an enthusiastic child, picking stories: sometimes recurring elements show up (trends). Only after we collate, distill and filter, do we get something that we can broadcast further.  

And yet the two antonyms of this knowledge are lonely and crowded – a loneliness proclaimed; an existence amongst a sea of jokes. If time loves the present, the nature of time is like an open-ended conversation between being and becoming – like a secret made visible. That inspiring concept calls me to explore the beautiful and the terrifying aspects of being an autonomous entity: How do I process my own identity through the filter of algorithms? I have tried – the AI tries to make me a pattern.  

Which brings you to the waveform of the present. The present is a hundred-headed beast that is crushing the onion of longing. Inside of it, we can't quite describe but we feel a river of memories that constantly runs: ghosts, things we've matured. I imagine you will find this heading E yourself: women, or men, maybe pre-we get that.  

I keep writing, my aura at times flickers like the neon signs in my hallway. In my own mind, I realise: you want the same feeling that I get from this: spontaneously  – that a greeting is something that can disturb that positivity.  

I don't find an end. I am not at the moment of articulating; the on final word is, my loneliness a thousand hook for a thread. So maybe because we can say things in multiple ways, we keep it open. Because, after all, life is never ending…  

And that is my free‑writing reflex: to remember that we are all scribbles on the wall of the universe, a story that grew out of sunrise,  sunset, and rain in between.  In this strange call, you are also a part of me, and in turn every conversation is interpret, breath in.  

The world is thick; and in the little details I found out that the meaning can be found if I read, again: a world of pixel, a world of fear, a world of love. This I leave with your audience: may we all read this onto our own transmissions.’
